verses.1: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, glosses humazah (from hamz, “breaking”) as a habitual false libeller and lumazah (from lamz, “flaw, defect, slander”) as nearly synonymous. Al-Layth distinguishes backbiting from face-to-face slander, while another view distinguishes verbal abuse from insulting gestures; the fuʿalah pattern denotes conduct made habitual. The next verse explains such a person as one who hoards and repeatedly counts wealth with pleasure. Its indefiniteness belittles wealth, which can only meet daily needs; a variant derives ʿaddadahu from ʿuddah, stockpiling against future adversity.

verses.3: Al-Mizan explains yaḥsabu as supposing wealth will ward off death in this world; although akhladahu is formally past, it bears a future sense because yaḥsabu is present. Far-fetched hope and attachment to worldly life make covetousness and accumulation endless, as though wealth secured immortality. The amassed and counted wealth produces a sense of self-sufficiency and superiority, hence transgression (96:7), which leads to slander and gossip. Verse 3 thus explains the hoarding and counting of verse 2, which explains the scandal-mongering of verse 1.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says kallā decisively refutes the belief that wealth preserves life, while the lām in la-yunbadhanna expresses an oath. Nabdh is to fling away, and al-ḥūṭamah is an intensive form from ḥaṭm, “breaking” or “cracking,” also defined as consuming; it is a name of hell, the fire of Allah set ablaze (104:6). Rather than becoming immortal, they will die and be flung into the Crusher.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the question magnifies the Crusher and inspires awe. Al-mūqadah, from īqād, is kindled fire. Taṭṭaliʿu, from iṭṭilāʿ, and ṭulūʿ mean rising, appearing, and hanging over; al-afʾidah is the plural of fuʾād, synonymous with qalb and, in Qur’anic usage, the principle of consciousness and reasoning—the human soul. Apparently this fire burns a person inwardly as well as outwardly, unlike worldly fire; its fuel is humans and stones (2:24).

verses.8: Al-Mizan says the fire will wholly surround its inhabitants, leaving no escape or refuge. Mumaddadh, from tamdīd, intensifies stretching or extending, and ʿamad is the plural of ʿamūd, a pillar, pole, or column. Reported possibilities are enclosing stakes, or huge extended shackles in which prisoners are locked, like perforated posts or tree trunks securing their feet; it notes that other views also exist.
